subject: chemistry
title: Reactions of acids
welcome_lead: Today's adventure: Reactions of acids — AQA GCSE Chemistry (8462) specification, section 4.4.2.
meta_desc: GCSE Chemistry (AQA) practice covering Reactions of acids, specification section 4.4.2.
final_note: You worked through Reactions of acids — 37 specification statements.

concepts.def: A compound formed when the hydrogen of an acid is replaced by a metal ion or by another positive ion. The acid supplies the negative ion and the metal, base, alkali or carbonate supplies the positive ion.
Acids react with some metals to produce a salt and hydrogen: for example Mg + 2HCl → MgCl₂ + H₂. The hydrogen is seen as bubbles of gas.
Only metals more reactive than hydrogen release hydrogen from a dilute acid. Magnesium, zinc and iron do; copper does not react with dilute hydrochloric or sulfuric acid.
Loss of electrons. When a metal reacts with an acid the metal atoms lose electrons to form positive ions, so the metal is oxidised.
Gain of electrons. In an acid-metal reaction the hydrogen ions gain electrons to become hydrogen molecules, so they are reduced.
A reaction in which electrons are transferred, so that oxidation and reduction happen together. Acid-metal reactions are redox reactions.
An equation showing the electrons lost or gained by one species, such as Mg → Mg²⁺ + 2e⁻ or 2H⁺ + 2e⁻ → H₂.
An ion that is present but unchanged by the reaction, such as the chloride ion when magnesium reacts with hydrochloric acid.
A substance that neutralises an acid to give a salt and water. Insoluble metal hydroxides and metal oxides are bases.
A base that dissolves in water, such as a soluble metal hydroxide. Its aqueous solution contains hydroxide ions.
The reaction of an acid with a base, alkali or carbonate in which the acid is used up and a salt is formed.
Metal carbonates neutralise acids to produce a salt, water and carbon dioxide, which is why the mixture fizzes.
The salt's name has two parts: the first comes from the positive ion of the base, alkali or carbonate, the second from the acid used.
Hydrochloric acid produces chlorides, nitric acid produces nitrates and sulfuric acid produces sulfates.
The positive ion in a salt comes from the base, alkali or carbonate, not from the acid and not from the water formed.
Acid + metal gives salt + hydrogen; acid + base or alkali gives salt + water; acid + carbonate gives salt + water + carbon dioxide.
Familiar ions used to build salt formulae include Na⁺, K⁺, Mg²⁺, Ca²⁺, Zn²⁺, Fe²⁺, Cu²⁺, Cl⁻, NO₃⁻, SO₄²⁻ and CO₃²⁻.
A salt formula is neutral overall, so the ions are combined in the ratio that cancels the charges, using brackets where a whole ion is repeated, as in Ca(NO₃)₂.
A soluble salt is made by reacting an acid with a solid insoluble metal, metal oxide, hydroxide or carbonate, then removing the unreacted solid.
Solid is added until no more reacts, which guarantees that all the acid has been used and none is left to contaminate the salt.
Separating an insoluble solid from a liquid using filter paper. The unreacted solid stays as the residue; the dissolved salt passes through as the filtrate.
Concentrating a salt solution by evaporating some of the water and then leaving it, so that crystals of the solid salt form as the rest evaporates.
Crystals that contain no unreacted acid or solid and no remaining water; they are patted dry between filter papers rather than heated hard.
Preparation of a pure, dry sample of a soluble salt from an insoluble oxide or carbonate, using a Bunsen burner to heat the dilute acid.
The gentle heating used to evaporate the salt solution in Required practical 1, so that the salt is not decomposed and crystals can form.
The ion that all acids produce in aqueous solution; it is what makes a solution acidic.
The ion present in aqueous solutions of alkalis; it is what makes a solution alkaline.
A scale from 0 to 14 measuring the acidity or alkalinity of a solution, measured with universal indicator or a pH probe.
An instrument that gives a numerical pH reading directly, more precisely than a colour chart can.
A solution with pH 7. Below 7 a solution is acidic, above 7 it is alkaline.
In neutralisation between an acid and an alkali, the hydrogen ions from the acid react with the hydroxide ions from the alkali to produce water.
H⁺ + OH⁻ → H₂O, the equation the specification gives for the reaction of hydrogen ions with hydroxide ions.
A wide range indicator whose colour is matched to a chart to give an approximate pH.
A measured pH is used to classify a solution: below 7 acidic, 7 neutral, above 7 alkaline.
A method of measuring the volumes of acid and alkali solutions that react with each other, using a suitable indicator.
The graduated tube that delivers the solution added a little at a time, read to the nearest 0.05 cm³.
Apparatus that delivers an accurate fixed volume, used with a safety filler to place the alkali in the conical flask.
The moment when the indicator changes colour permanently, showing that the acid and alkali have exactly reacted.
Titres that agree within 0.10 cm³. The rough titre is discarded and the mean is taken from the concordant results.
Amount of substance in moles divided by volume in dm³; volumes in cm³ are divided by 1000 first.
Mass in grams per dm³ of solution; it equals the concentration in mol/dm³ multiplied by Mᵣ.
An acid that is completely ionised in aqueous solution. Hydrochloric, nitric and sulfuric acids are strong acids.
An acid that is only partially ionised in aqueous solution. Ethanoic, citric and carbonic acids are weak acids.
The fraction of the acid molecules that have released their hydrogen ions. It is what strong and weak describe.
As pH falls by one unit the hydrogen ion concentration increases by a factor of 10.
A small amount of solute dissolved in a given volume of solution. Dilute is about amount, not about ionisation.
A large amount of solute dissolved in a given volume of solution. A weak acid can still be concentrated.
Comparing solutions by pH: the lower the whole-number pH, the greater the hydrogen ion concentration, with pH 7 as neutral.

mcqs.q: Dilute hydrochloric acid is added to a piece of magnesium ribbon. What are the products?
options: Magnesium chloride and hydrogen gas
Magnesium chloride and water
Magnesium chlorate plus hydrogen
Magnesium chloride, water and CO₂
mcqs.explain: Acids react with some metals to produce a salt and hydrogen; hydrochloric acid produces chlorides, so the salt is magnesium chloride.

mcqs.q: Pieces of magnesium, zinc, iron and copper are each added to dilute sulfuric acid. Only the copper gives no bubbles. Why?
options: Copper does react, but far too slowly to spot
Copper is too unreactive to release hydrogen
Copper makes a salt and water but no gas
Copper is a solid so acid cannot attack it
mcqs.explain: Acids react with only some metals. Copper is less reactive than hydrogen, so it cannot release hydrogen from the acid.

mcqs.q: Which equation correctly represents the reaction of zinc with dilute sulfuric acid?
options: Zn + H₂SO₄ → ZnSO₄ + H₂O
Zn + 2H₂SO₄ → ZnSO₄ + 2H₂
Zn + H₂SO₄ → ZnSO₄ + H₂
Zn + H₂SO₄ → ZnSO₄ + H
mcqs.explain: Sulfuric acid produces sulfates and the hydrogen is released as H₂. The equation is balanced as written.

mcqs.q: Iron filings are warmed with dilute hydrochloric acid. Which salt is formed?
options: Iron(III) chloride, FeCl₃
Iron(II) chlorate, Fe(ClO₃)₂
Iron(III) chloride, Fe₂Cl₆
Iron(II) chloride, FeCl₂
mcqs.explain: Dilute acid takes iron only as far as the Fe²⁺ ion, and two chloride ions balance that charge, giving FeCl₂.

mcqs.q: (HT) Why is the reaction between zinc and dilute hydrochloric acid described as a redox reaction?
options: Zinc gains electrons and hydrogen ions lose them
Zinc atoms lose electrons and hydrogen ions gain them
No oxygen is involved, so it is not a redox change
Hydrogen is released because acids contain hydrogen
mcqs.explain: Redox is defined by electron transfer: zinc is oxidised as it loses electrons and the hydrogen ions are reduced as they gain them.

mcqs.q: (HT) In the reaction Mg + 2HCl → MgCl₂ + H₂, which species is oxidised?
options: Hydrogen ions, as they lose electrons
Chloride ions, as they change place
Magnesium, as it loses two electrons
Magnesium, as it gains electrons
mcqs.explain: Each magnesium atom loses two electrons to form Mg²⁺, and loss of electrons is oxidation.

mcqs.q: (HT) Which line shows the reduction step when iron reacts with dilute sulfuric acid, and names it correctly?
options: Fe → Fe²⁺ + 2e⁻, the loss of electrons
H₂ → 2H⁺ + 2e⁻, written in reverse
Fe²⁺ + 2e⁻ → Fe, forming the iron metal
2H⁺ + 2e⁻ → H₂, a gain of electrons
mcqs.explain: The hydrogen ions gain electrons to form hydrogen molecules, and gain of electrons is reduction.

mcqs.q: Copper(II) oxide is added to warm dilute sulfuric acid. What is produced?
options: Copper sulfate and water only
Copper sulfate, water and hydrogen
Copper sulfate and carbon dioxide
Copper sulfide and water vapour
mcqs.explain: A metal oxide is a base, and acids are neutralised by bases to produce a salt and water only.

mcqs.q: Calcium carbonate chips are dropped into dilute nitric acid and the mixture fizzes. What are the three products?
options: Calcium nitrate and water, no gas
Calcium nitrate, water and hydrogen
Calcium nitrate, water and carbon dioxide
Calcium nitrite, water and CO₂ gas
mcqs.explain: Metal carbonates neutralise acids to produce a salt, water and carbon dioxide; nitric acid produces nitrates.

mcqs.q: Which substance is correctly described as an alkali?
options: Copper(II) oxide, which is an insoluble base
Copper hydroxide, which will not dissolve
Hydrochloric acid, which neutralises
Sodium hydroxide, a soluble metal hydroxide
mcqs.explain: An alkali is a base that dissolves in water, so a soluble metal hydroxide such as sodium hydroxide is an alkali.

mcqs.q: Which statement about the salts made by acids is correct?
options: Nitric acid produces nitrates
Sulfuric acid produces sulfides
Hydrochloric acid gives chlorates
Nitric acid yields nitrites
mcqs.explain: The acid used decides the salt: hydrochloric acid produces chlorides, nitric acid nitrates and sulfuric acid sulfates.

mcqs.q: Which pair of reactants would produce the salt potassium sulfate, K₂SO₄?
options: Hydrochloric acid and potassium hydroxide
Sulfuric acid and potassium hydroxide
Nitric acid and potassium hydroxide solution
Sulfuric acid and sodium hydroxide solution
mcqs.explain: The acid supplies the sulfate ion and the alkali supplies the potassium ions, giving K₂SO₄ and water.

mcqs.q: In a reaction between an acid and a base, where does the positive ion in the salt come from?
options: From the acid that is being used
From the water formed in the reaction
From the indicator that has been added
From the base, alkali or carbonate used
mcqs.explain: The acid supplies the negative ion of the salt and the base, alkali or carbonate supplies the positive metal ion.

mcqs.q: Predict the products of the reaction between dilute hydrochloric acid and zinc oxide.
options: Zinc chloride and water only
Zinc chloride and hydrogen gas
Zinc chlorate plus water
Zinc chloride and CO₂ gas
mcqs.explain: Zinc oxide is a base, so it neutralises the acid to give a salt and water; hydrochloric acid gives a chloride.

mcqs.q: Calcium ions are Ca²⁺ and nitrate ions are NO₃⁻. What is the formula of calcium nitrate?
options: CaNO₃
Ca(NO₃)₂
Ca₂(NO₃)₂
Ca(NO₃)(NO₃)
mcqs.explain: Two nitrate ions are needed to balance the 2+ charge on one calcium ion, and the bracket shows that both are nitrate ions.

mcqs.q: Zinc ions are Zn²⁺ and sulfate ions are SO₄²⁻. What is the formula of zinc sulfate?
options: Zn₂SO₄
Zn(SO₄)₂
ZnSO₄
Zn₂(SO₄)₂
mcqs.explain: The 2+ and 2− charges cancel one to one, so no extra subscripts are needed.

mcqs.q: When making a soluble salt, why is the insoluble solid added to the acid until no more reacts?
options: To be sure that all of the acid has been used up
To make the reaction happen much more quickly
To leave some spare acid to help crystals form
To dissolve the solid completely in the acid
mcqs.explain: Adding solid until some is left over guarantees that no acid remains in the solution to contaminate the salt.

mcqs.q: Which solid should be added to dilute sulfuric acid to prepare copper sulfate by this method?
options: Copper metal turnings
Copper(II) oxide powder
Sodium hydroxide solution
Solid copper sulfate
mcqs.explain: Copper metal is too unreactive, but copper(II) oxide is an insoluble base that neutralises the acid.

mcqs.q: After the excess solid has been filtered off, where is the salt?
options: Trapped in the residue left on the filter paper
Split evenly between the residue and the filtrate
Dissolved in the filtrate that passes through
Lost as a gas while the mixture is filtered
mcqs.explain: The salt is soluble, so it stays in solution and passes through the filter paper as the filtrate.

mcqs.q: Which sequence produces a pure, dry sample of a soluble salt from an insoluble base?
options: Filter the acid first, then add the solid oxide
Add excess acid, filter it, then crystallise
Add the solid, then boil the whole mixture dry
Add excess solid, filter, then crystallise
mcqs.explain: The excess solid removes all the acid, filtering removes that excess, and crystallising the filtrate gives the solid salt.

mcqs.q: How is a solution of a salt best turned into good crystals of the solid salt?
options: Boil the solution dry over a roaring flame
Evaporate some water, then leave it to crystallise
Add more water until crystals begin to appear
Filter the warm solution through paper twice
mcqs.explain: Salt solutions can be crystallised: the solution is concentrated, then left so that crystals form slowly as the rest of the water evaporates.

mcqs.q: In Required practical 1, how is the salt solution evaporated once the excess solid has been filtered off?
options: With a roaring Bunsen flame under the dish
By filtering the solution through paper
Using a water bath or an electric heater
By adding a drying agent to the liquid
mcqs.explain: The specification names a water bath or an electric heater for the evaporation step, giving gentle, controlled heating.

mcqs.q: Which ion do all acids produce in aqueous solution?
options: Hydroxide ions, OH⁻
Chloride ions, Cl⁻
Oxide ions, O²⁻
Hydrogen ions, H⁺
mcqs.explain: Acids produce hydrogen ions, H⁺, in aqueous solutions; this is what makes a solution acidic.

mcqs.q: What do aqueous solutions of alkalis contain?
options: Hydroxide ions, OH⁻
The hydrogen ions, H⁺
Hydrogen molecules, H₂
Water molecules only
mcqs.explain: Aqueous solutions of alkalis contain hydroxide ions, OH⁻, which is why they neutralise acids.

mcqs.q: Which statement about the pH scale is correct?
options: It runs from 1 to 14 and measures the acid strength
It runs from 0 to 7 for acids and no further
It runs from 0 to 14 and measures acidity or alkalinity
It runs from 0 to 14 and measures concentration
mcqs.explain: The pH scale, from 0 to 14, is a measure of the acidity or alkalinity of a solution.

mcqs.q: Four solutions have pH values of 2, 7, 9 and 13. Which statement is correct?
options: The solution at pH 2 must be alkaline and pH 13 acidic
The solution at pH 7 does not contain any ions
The solutions at pH 9 and pH 13 are both neutral
The solution at pH 2 is acidic and pH 13 is alkaline
mcqs.explain: Solutions with a pH below 7 are acidic and those above 7 are alkaline, so pH 2 is acidic and pH 13 alkaline.

mcqs.q: Which equation represents the neutralisation of an acid by an alkali?
options: H⁺ + OH⁻ → H₂O
H⁺ + OH⁻ → H₂O₂
2H⁺ + 2OH⁻ → H₂O
H⁺ + OH⁻ → H₂
mcqs.explain: In neutralisation between an acid and an alkali, hydrogen ions react with hydroxide ions to produce water.

mcqs.q: A few drops of universal indicator are added to a solution and the colour is matched to a chart. What does this give?
options: An exact pH value, correct to two decimal places
An approximate value for the solution's pH
The concentration of the acid in mol per dm³
The volume of alkali needed for neutralisation
mcqs.explain: Universal indicator, a wide range indicator, gives an approximate pH when its colour is matched to a chart.

mcqs.q: What is measured in a titration between an acid and an alkali?
options: The mass of salt made when they are mixed
The temperature rise during the reaction
The exact pH at every stage of the reaction
The volumes of the solutions that react together
mcqs.explain: Titration measures the volumes of acid and alkali solutions that react with each other, using a suitable indicator.

mcqs.q: In a titration, how should the 25.0 cm³ of alkali be measured into the conical flask?
options: With a pipette and a safety filler
With a measuring cylinder poured in
From the burette holding the acid
By weighing it out on a balance
mcqs.explain: A pipette delivers an accurate, fixed volume of alkali into the flask, and a filler is used instead of mouth suction.

mcqs.q: Why is a single indicator such as phenolphthalein used in a titration rather than universal indicator?
options: It shows the pH at every stage of the titration
It changes colour sharply at the end point
Universal indicator reacts with the acid used
It makes the neutralisation happen faster
mcqs.explain: A single indicator gives one sudden colour change, so the end point can be judged to the nearest drop.

mcqs.q: In Required practical 2, a student records titres of 24.10, 23.55 and 23.60 cm³. What should be done next?
options: Take the mean of all three titres recorded
Use the largest titre, because it is safest
Average the two concordant titres only
Repeat until the titres are all identical
mcqs.explain: The rough first titre is discarded and the mean is taken from the titres that agree within 0.10 cm³.

mcqs.q: (HT) How many moles are there in 20.0 cm³ of hydrochloric acid of concentration 0.100 mol/dm³?
options: 2.00 mol
200 mol
mcqs.explain: The volume in dm³ is 20.0 ÷ 1000 = 0.0200 dm³, so moles = 0.0200 × 0.100 = 0.00200 mol.

mcqs.q: (HT) 25.0 cm³ of sodium hydroxide is neutralised by 20.0 cm³ of 0.100 mol/dm³ hydrochloric acid, reacting 1:1. What is the concentration of the alkali?
options: 0.00800 mol/dm³
0.0800 mol/dm³
0.125 mol/dm³
0.05 mol/dm³
mcqs.explain: Moles of acid = 0.0200 × 0.100 = 0.00200 mol, so moles of alkali = 0.00200 mol and 0.00200 ÷ 0.0250 = 0.0800 mol/dm³.

mcqs.q: (HT) A sodium hydroxide solution has a concentration of 0.0800 mol/dm³. What is this in g/dm³? (Mᵣ of NaOH = 40)
options: 0.002 g/dm³
0.08 g/dm³
3.2 g/dm³
32 g/dm³
mcqs.explain: Concentration in g/dm³ = concentration in mol/dm³ × Mᵣ = 0.0800 × 40 = 3.2 g/dm³.

mcqs.q: (HT) What does it mean to say that hydrochloric acid is a strong acid?
options: It contains a large amount of acid in each dm³
It is no more ionised than a weak acid is
It will react with every metal that is added to it
It is completely ionised in aqueous solution
mcqs.explain: A strong acid is completely ionised in aqueous solution, so every acid molecule releases its hydrogen ion.

mcqs.q: (HT) Which set contains only weak acids?
options: Hydrochloric, nitric and sulfuric acids
Ethanoic acid, citric acid and carbonic acid
Ethanoic acid, nitric and sulfuric acids
Citric acid, carbonic acid and nitric acid
mcqs.explain: Ethanoic, citric and carbonic acids are the weak acids named in the specification; each is only partially ionised.

mcqs.q: (HT) A bottle is labelled 'concentrated ethanoic acid'. What does the word concentrated tell you?
options: The ethanoic acid in it is completely ionised
There is only a little acid dissolved in each dm³
A large amount of acid is dissolved in each dm³
It cannot be a weak acid when concentrated
mcqs.explain: Concentrated describes the amount of substance dissolved in a given volume; ethanoic acid is still a weak acid.

mcqs.q: (HT) The pH of a solution falls from 5 to 3. How does the hydrogen ion concentration change?
options: It increases by a factor of 2
It increases by a factor of 1000
It increases by a factor of ten only
It increases by a factor of 100
mcqs.explain: Each fall of one pH unit multiplies the hydrogen ion concentration by 10, so a fall of two units multiplies it by 100.

mcqs.q: (HT) Equal concentrations of hydrochloric acid and ethanoic acid are compared. Which has the lower pH, and why?
options: Hydrochloric acid, as it fully ionises
Ethanoic acid, as it ionises only partly
Hydrochloric acid, as it is more concentrated
Neither, as their concentrations are equal
mcqs.explain: For a given concentration, the stronger acid produces more hydrogen ions, so it has the lower pH.

mcqs.q: (HT) Solution X has pH 4 and solution Y has pH 7. What can be said about their hydrogen ion concentrations?
options: X has just 3 times the hydrogen ion concentration of Y
Y has the higher hydrogen ion concentration here
X has 1000 times the hydrogen ion concentration of Y
Both are neutral, so the two values must match
mcqs.explain: Three pH units below neutral means the hydrogen ion concentration is 10 × 10 × 10 = 1000 times greater.

specSource: AQA GCSE Chemistry (8462) specification; section 4.4.2 Reactions of acids
